---
title: "Aggregation"
subtitle: "Counting across sites without revealing the counts"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import os

os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")
```

Three hospitals each hold a patient cohort. A researcher wants to know
how many patients across all three match a clinical criterion. No
hospital will disclose its own count.

Each site counts locally, encrypts that single integer under the
coordinator's public key, and sends the ciphertext. The coordinator
adds the ciphertexts homomorphically and decrypts only the total.

## The protocol

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples import aggregation

result = aggregation.run()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
from IPython.display import Markdown

Markdown(f"""
| | value |
|---|---|
| site cohort sizes | {result.site_sizes} |
| per-site counts *(never seen by the coordinator)* | {result.per_site_cleartext} |
| **encrypted total** | **{result.total_encrypted}** |
| cleartext total | {result.total_cleartext} |
""")
```

The recovered total is `{python} result.total_encrypted`, matching the
cleartext sum `{python} result.total_cleartext` **exactly**.

## Why exactly, and not approximately

The scheme here is BFV, which does exact integer arithmetic. A count
is an integer, so the answer is the integer — not a value close to it.
CKKS, used elsewhere in these examples for real-valued work, trades
exactness for the ability to encrypt real numbers, and there
comparisons carry a tolerance. Here `==` is the right test and the
code asserts it.

```{python}
assert result.exact
assert result.total_encrypted == sum(result.per_site_cleartext)
```

## What the coordinator learns

Only the total. The per-site counts
(`{python} str(result.per_site_cleartext)`) exist inside each site and
in this document, which stands in for all three parties at once — but
never in the coordinator's view of the protocol.

There is a limit to that guarantee, and it is worth stating plainly:
the coordinator holds the secret key. If a site's ciphertext were sent
on its own, the coordinator *could* decrypt it. The protocol relies on
the coordinator only ever seeing the sum.

[Query counting](query-count.qmd) removes that reliance. There the key
is split across sites, so the coordinator cannot decrypt anything
alone — the same computation, a stronger guarantee.
